A whinny is a sound — specifically, the soft, gentle, high-pitched, trembling cry that a horse makes.
What exactly does it sound like?

Imagine a horse making a musical, quivering sound from its throat — something like a series of short, vibrating tones strung together. It's breathy, light, and somewhat melodic. It is not a sharp, loud, or startling sound. It has a warm, almost gentle quality to it.

If you've ever been near a horse and heard it make a soft, fluttery vocal sound — that is a whinny.
How is it different from a "neigh"?

This is an important distinction, because learners often confuse these two words.

A neigh is the loud, full, powerful call of a horse — the kind you'd hear from a distance, the kind that rings out dramatically. Think of a war horse or a horse rearing up in a movie.

A whinny is softer and quieter than a neigh. It's more intimate, more subdued. Some people describe a whinny as a small neigh. While the two words are sometimes used interchangeably in everyday writing, strictly speaking, a whinny carries the sense of gentleness and softness that a neigh does not.

In practice: a horse might neigh to alert others from far away, but it might whinny when it recognizes its owner walking into the stable.
When do horses make this sound?

Horses produce a whinny in several situations:

  • Greeting — when they see a familiar person or another horse they know
  • Calling out — when looking for a companion that has moved out of sight
  • Mild excitement or anticipation — such as when it's feeding time and the horse senses food is coming
  • Expressing mild distress — a soft, worried call when something feels slightly off

So a whinny is communicative. It's how a horse "speaks" in a soft, non-aggressive way.
Is this word used for animals other than horses?

Primarily, yes — whinny is almost exclusively associated with horses. Occasionally, writers use it loosely for related animals like donkeys or zebras, but if you say "whinny," people will immediately picture a horse.
The plural of whinny is whinnies — the y changes to ies, following the standard English spelling rule.

• The old mare gave a soft whinny when she heard the farmer's footsteps.
  • From inside the barn came the gentle whinnies of the horses settling in for the night.
  • The foal's whinny grew louder as it searched for its mother.
  • He hadn't visited in months, but the horse still recognized him — it let out a small, happy whinny the moment he opened the gate.

A whinny (noun) is the soft, gentle, trembling vocal sound made by a horse — lighter and quieter than a neigh, used to communicate gently, greet, or call out. When you read this word, picture a horse making a warm, fluttery, musical sound, not a dramatic or loud one. That image will serve you correctly every time.
